E-commerce Customer Analytics¶

Analysing customer purchasing behaviour, revenue drivers and service quality for a Southeast-Asian online retailer
Author Sak
Tools Python 3, Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn, SciPy
Dataset data/raw/ecommerce_orders_raw.csv — 2,045 order records, and data/raw/products.csv — a 60-product catalogue (both synthetic, generated by src/generate_dataset.py)
Period covered January 2024 – June 2025

1. Problem Definition & Project Scope¶

1.1 Business problem¶

An online retailer selling across seven Southeast-Asian markets has grown quickly but has never analysed its order history systematically. Management does not know which products, customer groups and markets actually drive revenue, whether customers come back after their first purchase, or why some customers leave poor reviews and return products. Marketing budget is spread evenly across channels and product categories, and decisions are made on intuition.

This project turns the raw order log into evidence-based answers to those questions so the business can focus its marketing, inventory and logistics efforts where they have the most impact.

1.2 Project scope¶

In scope

  • Order-level transaction data from 1 January 2024 to 30 June 2025 (18 months).
  • Customer attributes attached to each order: age, gender, country, city, sign-up date, segment and acquisition channel.
  • Order attributes: product (with its category and subcategory), quantity, unit price, discount, shipping cost, payment method, device, delivery time, order status and review rating.
  • A product catalogue of 60 products in 7 categories and 30 subcategories (e.g. Books → Comics & Manga, Programming, Fiction), each with one fixed list price and its current stock on hand.
  • Data cleaning (missing values, duplicates, validation), feature engineering, descriptive & statistical analysis, and visualisation with Pandas / Matplotlib / Seaborn.

Out of scope

  • Cost of goods, profit margin, and marketing spend (not available in the dataset).
  • Predictive / machine-learning modelling (e.g. churn prediction) — this project is descriptive and diagnostic only.
  • Web-analytics events (page views, cart abandonment) — only completed orders are analysed.

2. Objectives & Analytical Questions¶

2.1 Measurable objectives¶

# Objective Success measure
O1 Identify the main revenue drivers. Quantify how revenue is distributed across product categories, subcategories and products, customer segments, countries and acquisition channels. Revenue share (%) per category / segment / country / channel, and identification of the groups that together produce ≥ 80 % of revenue.
O2 Measure customer retention and value concentration. Determine what proportion of customers are repeat buyers and how concentrated spending is among top customers. Repeat-purchase rate (%), share of revenue from the top 20 % of customers, share of customers flagged as churn-risk.
O3 Diagnose service-quality problems. Test whether delivery speed and product returns are related to customer satisfaction (review rating). Correlation coefficient between delivery_days and review_rating, mean rating by delivery-time band, return rate (%) per category.

2.2 Analytical questions¶

# Question Technique
Q1 Which product categories generate the most revenue, and which have the highest return rates? groupby + agg, sorting
Q2 How do customer segments (New / Regular / VIP) differ in order frequency, order value and total spend? groupby, derived customer table
Q3 How do orders and revenue trend month by month — is there seasonality? time-series groupby, line chart
Q4 Which countries and acquisition channels bring the most valuable customers? groupby, pivot_table
Q5 Does delivery time affect the review rating customers give? correlation, binning, box plot
Q6 What share of customers are repeat buyers, and how many are at risk of churning? customer-level aggregation, RFM-style flags
Q7 Do device usage and payment preferences differ across age groups? crosstab
Q8 Which products and subcategories sell best, and which products are about to run out of stock? multi-key groupby, stock-cover calculation

3. Dataset & Data Dictionary¶

The dataset was produced by src/generate_dataset.py, a reproducible generator (seed = 42) that first builds a product catalogue (60 products, each with a fixed price and a stock level), then simulates 2,000 orders of those products from 724 customers, and finally deliberately injects realistic data-quality problems: missing values, 45 exact duplicate rows, out-of-range numbers (negative ages, ratings above 5, discounts above 100 %, etc.) inconsistent category spelling, product names in the wrong case and prices that disagree with the catalogue. The full data dictionary is also available in docs/data_dictionary.md.

Product catalogue (products.csv): product_id, product_name, category, subcategory (30 in total, e.g. Comics & Manga, Programming), unit_price (fixed list price), stock_on_hand (units in stock at 30 June 2025) and reorder_level (10 units).

Added during cleaning (Section 8): subcategory, looked up from the catalogue.

Derived columns created in Section 9: gross_amount, discount_amount, total_amount, net_revenue, customer_tenure_days, age_group, order_value_tier, order_month, order_weekday, is_returned, has_review.

Interpretation. The raw file contains 2,045 rows × 22 columns and the catalogue 60 products in 7 categories and 30 subcategories — each category has 5–13 products, so Books, for example, splits into Comics & Manga, Programming, Fiction, Self-Help and Children's. df.info() shows several columns with missing data (age, city, unit_price, payment_method, delivery_days, review_rating). df.describe() immediately flags impossible values: the minimum age is −5 and the maximum 210, quantity goes down to −2, discount_pct reaches 150 %, unit_price has negative values (as low as −$100), delivery_days ranges from −3 to 60, and review_rating spans 0 to 7 even though the valid scale is 1–5. The categorical summary shows product_category has 19 unique values instead of 7 (inconsistent capitalisation / whitespace), product_name has 69 values for 60 products, and gender has 4 values instead of 2. All of these are dealt with in Sections 6–8.

Interpretation & handling strategy. Missing values fall into two very different groups:

  1. Structurally missing (not an error). delivery_days is empty for every cancelled order (a cancelled order is never delivered), and review_rating is empty for all cancelled orders and for roughly a third of delivered / returned orders (customers simply did not leave a review). These blanks carry information, so they are kept as NaN rather than invented. Analyses on rating use only the rows that have a rating.
  2. Genuinely missing attributes (data-entry / export errors). age (~3 %), payment_method (~2 %), city (~1.5 %) and unit_price (~1 %) are missing at random in small proportions. The handling rule per column is:
Column Method Rationale
age Median imputation Numeric and contains outliers (see Section 8); the median is robust to those outliers, unlike the mean.
payment_method Mode imputation Categorical; the most frequent method is the most likely value. Only 2 % of rows are affected so bias is negligible.
city Mode within country City depends on country, so imputing the most common city of the same country is more accurate than a global mode.
unit_price Look-up from the product catalogue Every product has one fixed list price, so a missing price is not unknown — it is the catalogue price of that product_id. This is exact, not an estimate, so no order has to be dropped.

Imputation is applied after de-duplication and validation (Sections 7–8) so that duplicates and invalid values do not distort the medians / modes used for filling.

df = df.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Rows before: {n_before:,}  |  duplicates removed: {n_dup_exact}  |  rows remaining: {len(df):,}")
assert df["order_id"].is_unique, "order_id should now be unique"

Rows before: 2,045  |  duplicates removed: 45  |  rows remaining: 2,000

Interpretation. After standardising text, 45 exact duplicate rows were found, and each duplicated order_id matched an exact duplicate row — i.e. these are pure double-exports rather than legitimately repeated orders. They were removed with drop_duplicates(), leaving 2,000 unique orders. Had we not standardised the text first, some duplicates whose category differed only in capitalisation would have escaped detection.

8. Data Validation¶

We check data types, category domains and numeric value ranges against explicit business rules.

In [13]:
RULES = {                      # column: (min allowed, max allowed)
    "age":           (18, 100),
    "quantity":      (1, 50),
    "unit_price":    (0.01, 5000),
    "discount_pct":  (0, 100),
    "shipping_cost": (0, 100),
    "delivery_days": (0, 30),
    "review_rating": (1, 5),
}
VALID_CATEGORIES = ["Electronics", "Fashion", "Home & Kitchen", "Beauty", "Sports", "Books", "Toys"]
VALID_STATUS     = ["Delivered", "Cancelled", "Returned"]

# --- 8.1 data types -------------------------------------------------------
print(df.dtypes, "\n")

# --- 8.2 categorical domains ---------------------------------------------
print("Invalid product_category :", (~df["product_category"].isin(VALID_CATEGORIES)).sum())
print("Invalid order_status     :", (~df["order_status"].isin(VALID_STATUS)).sum())
print("Invalid gender           :", (~df["gender"].isin(["Female", "Male"])).sum())

# --- 8.2b every order must reference a real product, at that product's fixed price
list_price = df["product_id"].map(products.set_index("product_id")["unit_price"])
print("Unknown product_id       :", (~df["product_id"].isin(products["product_id"])).sum())
print("Price differs from list  :", (df["unit_price"].notna() & ~np.isclose(df["unit_price"], list_price)).sum())
print("Price missing            :", df["unit_price"].isna().sum())

# --- 8.3 numeric ranges ---------------------------------------------------
report = []
for col, (lo, hi) in RULES.items():
    bad = df[col].notna() & ((df[col] < lo) | (df[col] > hi))
    report.append({"column": col, "min_allowed": lo, "max_allowed": hi,
                   "observed_min": df[col].min(), "observed_max": df[col].max(),
                   "invalid_rows": int(bad.sum())})
validation_report = pd.DataFrame(report)

# --- 8.5 Fix: invalid values are impossible, so treat them as missing ...
for col, (lo, hi) in RULES.items():
    bad = df[col].notna() & ((df[col] < lo) | (df[col] > hi))
    df.loc[bad, col] = np.nan

# ... then drop rows whose quantity is unusable (revenue can't be computed without it)
critical = df["quantity"].isna()
print(f"Rows dropped (missing/invalid quantity): {critical.sum()}")
df = df[~critical].reset_index(drop=True)

# --- 8.5b The catalogue is the source of truth for product name, category and price:
# a missing or wrong price is restored from the list price instead of dropping the order.
ref = products.set_index("product_id")
list_price = df["product_id"].map(ref["unit_price"])
restored = df["unit_price"].isna() | ~np.isclose(df["unit_price"].fillna(-1), list_price)
print(f"Prices restored from the catalogue: {restored.sum()}")
print(f"Product names fixed               : {(df['product_name'] != df['product_id'].map(ref['product_name'])).sum()}")
df["unit_price"] = list_price
df["product_name"] = df["product_id"].map(ref["product_name"])
df["product_category"] = df["product_id"].map(ref["category"])
df.insert(df.columns.get_loc("product_category") + 1, "subcategory", df["product_id"].map(ref["subcategory"]))

# --- 8.6 Impute the remaining missing attributes (strategy from Section 6)
df["age"] = df["age"].fillna(df["age"].median())
df["payment_method"] = df["payment_method"].fillna(df["payment_method"].mode()[0])
df["city"] = df.groupby("country")["city"].transform(lambda s: s.fillna(s.mode()[0]))
df["discount_pct"] = df["discount_pct"].fillna(0)                      # invalid discount -> no discount
not_cancelled = df["order_status"] != "Cancelled"
df.loc[not_cancelled, "delivery_days"] = df.loc[not_cancelled, "delivery_days"] \
                                           .fillna(df.loc[not_cancelled, "delivery_days"].median())

# Convert to appropriate types
df["age"] = df["age"].astype(int)
df["quantity"] = df["quantity"].astype(int)
for c in ["gender", "country", "customer_segment", "acquisition_channel",
          "product_category", "subcategory", "payment_method", "device_type", "order_status"]:
    df[c] = df[c].astype("category")

print(f"\nClean dataset: {df.shape[0]:,} rows x {df.shape[1]} columns")
df.isnull().sum()[lambda s: s > 0]

Rows dropped (missing/invalid quantity): 5
Prices restored from the catalogue: 23
Product names fixed               : 10

Clean dataset: 1,995 rows x 23 columns
Out[15]:
delivery_days    131
review_rating    748
dtype: int64

Interpretation. Validation found 25 out-of-range values across seven numeric fields (6 impossible ages, 5 non-positive quantities, 3 negative prices, 4 discounts outside 0–100 %, 3 implausible delivery times and 4 ratings outside 1–5), no domain violations after text standardisation and no orders dated before sign-up. Every order references a real product, but 23 prices disagreed with the catalogue (20 missing, 3 negative) and 10 product names were in the wrong case. Impossible values were treated as missing; the 5 rows with an invalid quantity were dropped because revenue cannot be computed without it. Prices, however, were restored from the catalogue instead of dropping those orders — the list price is known exactly — and names and categories were reset to the catalogue spelling, with subcategory added. The clean dataset has 1,995 orders, and the only remaining NaNs are the structural ones — delivery_days for cancelled orders and review_rating where no review was left.

9. Derived / Calculated Columns¶

In [16]:
# --- Monetary fields ------------------------------------------------------
df["gross_amount"]    = (df["quantity"] * df["unit_price"]).round(2)
df["discount_amount"] = (df["gross_amount"] * df["discount_pct"] / 100).round(2)
df["total_amount"]    = (df["gross_amount"] - df["discount_amount"] + df["shipping_cost"]).round(2)
# Net revenue: cancelled and returned orders are refunded, so they contribute 0
df["net_revenue"]     = np.where(df["order_status"] == "Delivered", df["total_amount"], 0.0)

# --- Customer & time fields ----------------------------------------------
df["customer_tenure_days"] = (df["order_date"] - df["signup_date"]).dt.days
df["age_group"] = pd.cut(df["age"], bins=[17, 24, 34, 44, 54, 100],
                         labels=["18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55+"])
df["order_value_tier"] = pd.cut(df["total_amount"], bins=[-np.inf, 50, 150, 400, np.inf],
                                labels=["Low (<$50)", "Medium ($50-150)", "High ($150-400)", "Premium (>$400)"])
df["order_month"]   = df["order_date"].dt.to_period("M").astype(str)
df["order_weekday"] = df["order_date"].dt.day_name()

# --- Flags ----------------------------------------------------------------
df["is_returned"] = (df["order_status"] == "Returned").astype(int)
df["has_review"]  = df["review_rating"].notna().astype(int)

df[["order_id", "quantity", "unit_price", "discount_pct", "shipping_cost",
    "gross_amount", "discount_amount", "total_amount", "net_revenue",
    "customer_tenure_days", "age_group", "order_value_tier"]].head(8)

Interpretation. Eleven new columns were derived (plus subcategory, added from the catalogue). The most important are total_amount (what the customer paid: quantity × list price − discount + shipping) and net_revenue (revenue the business actually keeps, which is zero for cancelled and returned orders). age_group and order_value_tier turn continuous variables into bands that make grouping and cross-tabulation readable, while customer_tenure_days measures how long a customer had been registered when they placed each order.

10. Data Analysis with Pandas¶

Each sub-section answers one of the analytical questions using filtering, sorting, grouping, aggregation, pivot tables and crosstabs.

Interpretation. Over 18 months the retailer processed 1,995 valid orders from 723 customers, earning ≈ $149 k** in net revenue. The average order is worth **$92 but the median is only $50, a sign that a minority of large (mostly Electronics) orders pull the mean up. Roughly 1 in 9 orders is returned (11.2 %) and 6.6 % are cancelled, so about 18 % of orders generate no revenue at all — a leakage worth investigating. Customers leave a review on 63 % of orders, with an average rating of 3.53 / 5.

Interpretation (Q1). Revenue is heavily concentrated: Electronics alone produces 47 % of net revenue from only 24 % of orders, because its average order value ($186) is 2–5× that of other categories ($35–$91). Electronics, Home & Kitchen and Fashion together deliver ≈ 77 % of revenue (objective O1). Books and Toys are low-value categories contributing under 8 % combined. Returns tell a different story: Fashion has the highest return rate (15.7 %), followed by Toys and Electronics (≈ 12 %); Books (7.1 %) and Beauty (8.0 %) are returned least. Fashion's combination of moderate revenue and the highest return rate makes it the priority for sizing / product-description improvements.

Interpretation (Q2). VIP customers are 23 % of the customer base but generate 40 % of revenue. They place 4.9 orders each on average versus 2.5 for Regular and 1.6 for New customers, and each VIP is worth **≈ $353** in net revenue — about 1.9× a Regular customer and 2.8× a New customer. Average order value is similar across segments (VIP is actually the lowest at $87), so the difference comes entirely from purchase frequency, not basket size. VIPs also receive the largest average discounts (≈ 9.1 % vs 7.6–7.9 % for other segments), which is worth monitoring so that loyalty pricing does not erode margin.

Interpretation (Q7). Mobile is the main device for every age band under 55 (55–63 % of orders), with desktop second; the 45–54 group is actually the most mobile (63 %). A mobile-first checkout that keeps card and E-Wallet options prominent serves almost every customer.

# Stock cover: how many months the current stock lasts at the last 6 months' sales rate
cutoff = df["order_date"].max() - pd.DateOffset(months=6)
recent = df[(df["order_date"] > cutoff) & (df["order_status"] == "Delivered")]
stock = products.set_index("product_id")[["product_name", "category", "unit_price", "stock_on_hand", "reorder_level"]].copy()
stock["units_per_month"] = (recent.groupby("product_id")["quantity"].sum() / 6).reindex(stock.index).fillna(0).round(1)
stock["months_of_cover"] = (stock["stock_on_hand"] / stock["units_per_month"].replace(0, np.nan)).round(1)
stock["action"] = np.select([stock["stock_on_hand"] == 0,
                             (stock["stock_on_hand"] <= stock["reorder_level"]) | (stock["months_of_cover"] < 1)],
                            ["Sold out - reorder now", "Reorder"], "OK")
print(stock["action"].value_counts().to_string(), "\n")
stock.sort_values("months_of_cover").head(10)

Interpretation (Q8). Revenue is concentrated in a few products: the Smartphone A54 alone earns $16.6 k (11 % of all net revenue)**, and the top 10 of the 60 products produce **51 %**. High-priced Electronics dominate the ranking, but the **4L Air Fryer ($7.4 k) is the best non-Electronics product, and it is the main reason Small Appliances carries 60 % of Home & Kitchen revenue. By volume the leader is different — Wireless Earbuds sold 128 units, more than any other product. Within Books, Comics & Manga (30 %) and Programming (29 %) are the strongest subcategories. Some top sellers have high return rates (Smartphone 22 %, Slim-Fit Jeans 24 %), so a product-level return review is worthwhile. Stock needs action: 2 products are sold out — Noise-Cancelling Headphones (≈ 5 units/month, ≈ $775 of monthly revenue at risk) and the LED Table Lamp — and 4 more are at or below their reorder level with ≤ 3 months of cover (Matte Lipstick, Rice Cooker, Running Sneakers, Art & Craft Kit).

Interpretation. total_amount is strongly right-skewed (skewness ≈ 5.6): the mean ($92) is almost double the median ($50) and the standard deviation ($143) exceeds the mean, so a few very large orders dominate the spread. This is why the median is the better "typical order" figure. `unit_price` has only 60 possible values (one per product) and is also right-skewed, with a median of $29. Review ratings cluster around 4 (median and mode = 4, mean 3.53), delivery takes a median of 6 days, and the typical customer is 34 years old with a fairly symmetric age distribution (SD ≈ 10 years).

# --- Significance tests --------------------------------------------------
# 1. Delivery days vs rating (Pearson & Spearman)
r, p = stats.pearsonr(rated["delivery_days"], rated["review_rating"])
rho, p_s = stats.spearmanr(rated["delivery_days"], rated["review_rating"])
print(f"Delivery days vs rating: Pearson r = {r:.3f} (p = {p:.2e}); Spearman rho = {rho:.3f} (p = {p_s:.2e})")

# 2. Do VIP customers have a different average order value than New customers? (Welch t-test)
vip = df.loc[df["customer_segment"] == "VIP", "total_amount"]
new = df.loc[df["customer_segment"] == "New", "total_amount"]
t, p_t = stats.ttest_ind(vip, new, equal_var=False)
print(f"AOV VIP (${vip.mean():.2f}) vs New (${new.mean():.2f}): Welch t = {t:.2f}, p = {p_t:.3f}")

# 3. Is return status independent of product category? (Chi-square test)
ct = pd.crosstab(df["product_category"], df["is_returned"])
chi2, p_chi, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
print(f"Return vs category: chi2 = {chi2:.2f}, dof = {dof}, p = {p_chi:.3f}")

# 4. Does average rating differ between delivery bands? (one-way ANOVA)
groups = [g["review_rating"].values for _, g in rated.groupby("delivery_band", observed=True)]
f, p_f = stats.f_oneway(*groups)
print(f"Rating across delivery bands: ANOVA F = {f:.2f}, p = {p_f:.2e}")

Delivery days vs rating: Pearson r = -0.406 (p = 9.67e-51); Spearman rho = -0.408 (p = 2.98e-51)
AOV VIP ($86.73) vs New ($97.28): Welch t = -1.14, p = 0.255
Return vs category: chi2 = 15.83, dof = 6, p = 0.015
Rating across delivery bands: ANOVA F = 75.04, p = 1.31e-44

Interpretation. The correlation matrix shows total_amount is driven by unit_price (r = 0.84) and quantity (r = 0.33), as expected; shipping_cost is negatively related to order value (r = −0.44) because shipping is free above $120. Age, tenure and discount have essentially no linear relationship with order value (|r| < 0.05), so basket size is not explained by demographics. The one substantive behavioural relationship is delivery time vs rating: r ≈ −0.41 with p ≪ 0.001, and the ANOVA across delivery bands is likewise highly significant — slower delivery reliably lowers ratings. In contrast, the difference in average order value between VIP and New customers is not statistically significant (p = 0.26), confirming that VIP value comes from frequency rather than bigger baskets. The chi-square test does find a significant association between category and return status (p = 0.015), so the higher return rates of Fashion, Toys and Electronics are unlikely to be chance.

Interpretation. Both orders (bars) and revenue (line) rise through 2024 and spike in November–December, with December 2024 revenue ($13.3 k) about 1.6× the $8.3 k monthly average. The steep drop in January–February 2025 is the post-holiday trough, after which activity recovers to a level above the equivalent months of 2024. Revenue is more volatile than order count because a handful of high-value Electronics orders (a laptop is $649) can swing a month's total — e.g. the March 2025 jump.

The mean ($92) sits well to the right of the median ($50) because of that tail. For reporting "typical" customer spend the median is the safer measure, and pricing or free-shipping threshold decisions should be based on where the bulk of orders actually sit (the $20–$80 range).

13. Key Findings & Recommendations¶

13.1 Key findings (evidence-based)¶

# Finding Evidence
F1 Revenue is highly concentrated in Electronics — and in a handful of products. One category produces almost half of all revenue; three categories produce ≈ 77 %. Electronics = 47 % of net revenue from 24 % of orders; AOV $186 vs $35–$91 elsewhere. The top 10 of 60 products = 51 % of revenue; the Smartphone A54 alone = 11 % (Sections 10.2, 10.9, Charts 1 & 10).
F2 VIP customers drive value through frequency, not basket size. VIPs = 23 % of customers, 40 % of revenue, 4.9 orders each vs 1.6 for New; AOV difference VIP vs New not significant (p = 0.26) (Sections 10.3, 11, Chart 6).
F3 Slow delivery measurably hurts satisfaction. Rating falls from 3.97 (1–3 days) to 3.00 (10+ days); Pearson r = −0.41, p < 0.001; ANOVA significant (Sections 10.6, 11, Chart 5).
F4 Almost one in five orders produces no revenue, and returns depend on the category. 11.2 % returned + 6.6 % cancelled = 17.8 % of orders; Fashion returns 15.7 % vs Books 7.1 %; chi-square p = 0.015 (Sections 10.1, 10.2, 11, Charts 4 & 7).
F5 Strong year-end seasonality with a post-holiday slump. December 2024 = 184 orders / $13.3 k (≈ 2.4× the Q1 2024 monthly average); January 2025 revenue −45 % MoM (Section 10.4, Chart 2).
F6 Retention is good but a large share of customers has gone quiet. 67 % repeat-purchase rate and top 20 % of customers = 59 % of revenue, yet 45 % of customers have not ordered in 180+ days; New customers only 40 % repeat (Section 10.7).
F7 Referral brings the least valuable customers; Email the most. Revenue per customer: Email $246, Organic Search $217, Referral $145 (29 % below average) (Section 10.5).
F8 Stock gaps are already costing sales. 2 of 60 products are sold out (Noise-Cancelling Headphones sells ≈ 5 units / month ≈ $775 revenue), 4 more are at or below their reorder level with ≤ 3 months of cover (Section 10.9).

13.2 Recommendations (actionable)¶

# Recommendation Linked finding Expected impact / how to measure
R1 Set a delivery-time SLA of ≤ 5 days for the top markets (Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand) — renegotiate courier contracts or add a regional fulfilment hub — and show estimated delivery dates at checkout. F3 Each day saved ≈ +0.12 star; target average rating from 3.53 to ≥ 3.9 within two quarters.
R2 Launch a second-purchase programme for New customers: an automated email/e-wallet voucher 14 days after the first delivered order, plus a win-back campaign for the 45 % of customers inactive > 180 days. F2, F6 Raise New-customer repeat rate from 40 % toward the Regular level (71 %); track repeat rate and 180-day recency monthly.
R3 Reduce Fashion returns: add size guides, fit-based reviews and more product photos, starting with the products returned most (Slim-Fit Denim Jeans 24 %, Linen Blouse 20 %); record return reasons. F4 Bring Fashion returns from 15.7 % to the overall average (~11 %); track return rate per product monthly.
R4 Diversify revenue away from Electronics by cross-selling Home & Kitchen appliances (Air Fryer, Rice Cooker) and Sports bundles to Electronics buyers. F1 Reduce Electronics share below 45 % while growing total revenue; monitor category revenue share quarterly.
R5 Plan inventory and marketing around the seasonal curve: build Electronics stock and ad budget for Nov–Dec, and run a January "new-year" promotion to soften the post-holiday drop. F1, F5 Reduce the Jan/Feb revenue trough (currently −45 % MoM) to ≤ −30 %.
R6 Rebalance acquisition spend: shift part of the Referral budget to Email and Organic Search, and pay referral rewards only after the referred customer's second order. F7 Raise revenue per Referral customer above $200.
R7 Reorder automatically from the stock-cover table: restock the 2 sold-out products now, and reorder any product whose stock falls below 2 months of sales (the web app's Products page flags these). F8 Zero sold-out top-20 products; track lost revenue from stock-outs.

13.3 Limitations & next steps¶

  • The dataset is synthetic (generated to mimic realistic patterns) and contains no cost or margin data, so recommendations are framed around revenue, not profit.
  • Prices are fixed per product for the whole period; real catalogues change prices and run promotions, which would need a price-history table.
  • Next steps: build a churn-prediction model on the customer table, add return reasons and marketing-spend data, and automate this notebook as a monthly report.
